description:
Solo AI Engineer tackling the Flame in Freefall challenge: turning decades of NASA’s microgravity combustion research into clear, actionable fire safety insights for human space exploration.

Our focus is explainable AI (XAI) — every insight our dashboard surfaces is traceable back to its source investigation and publication in NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database, so researchers can trust, verify, and build on what the system tells them, rather than seeing as a black box
summary: NASA's PSI combustion archive is hard to find, compare and interpret. FLAMSA is an AI dashboard for students, researchers and engineers: 1,132 PSI files (864 MiB, 15 investigations) cleaned into 1,615 test records and a curated 20-PDF index. Click an oxygen and pressure point; a validated copilot ranks the closest NASA experiments and traces every claim to its source document in one click.
details:
Source Code Link: https://github.com/Huarada/FLAMSA

Challenge: Flame in Freefall. NASA's PSI archive holds the evidence for fire safety in crewed habitats, but, in NASA's own words, it is "hard to find, harder to compare, and harder yet to interpret". FLAMSA is an AI-powered dashboard that turns that archive into interactive, source-traced answers.

Who it is for

The audience named in the challenge: professors, graduate and undergraduate students, aerospace researchers and aerospace engineers. In the US alone there are about 68,700 aerospace engineers (BLS, 2025), projected to reach 74,400 by 2035. A second audience is engineers at commercial crewed-vehicle companies, who must assess material flammability under NASA-STD-6001.

Why it helps, and how we win users

A student or engineer who needed days to find the right experiment gets a ranked, cited shortlist in minutes, with the physics explained in plain language and the original document one click away. We start with classrooms and research groups, where one shared link replaces a repository search, and we widen to industry teams that need NASA evidence for their own oxygen and pressure conditions. Trust is the hook: every answer states what the data support and what they do not.

The physics behind the charts

Burning rate (FLEX). A burning droplet follows the d-squared law, and we estimate how its burning-rate constant K changes with oxygen, adjusting for pressure and droplet size:

d(t)² = d₀² − K·t

K = β₀ + β_O₂·O₂ + β_P·P + β_d·d₀ + ε

Atmosphere change (BASS-II). Gas readings before (i) and after (f) the same burn, in percentage points:

ΔO₂ = O₂,i − O₂,f

ΔCO₂ = CO₂,f − CO₂,i

Every chart states its units, tested ranges, 95% uncertainty intervals and source rows. They show evidence of burning behavior, not a risk classification.

The NASA data we consumed and how we treated it

  • 1,132 files, 864 MiB of the PSI archive for 15 combustion investigations (ACME, BASS, CFI, FLEX, SAFFIRE, SAME, SLICE, SPICE and more): 732 PDFs, 317 ISA-Tab metadata files, 41 spreadsheets and CSV tables, 14 videos and slide decks. The archive is kept read-only and is never modified.
  • 1,615 curated test records (1,556 individual tests; 693 with both oxygen and pressure, plotted on the coverage map). We normalized messy headers, units in headers or values, summary rows and empty cells into canonical units (psi, % O₂, cm/s, mm, s). The raw value always stays next to the normalized one, a missing value is never invented, and each source file is pinned by SHA-256.
  • We closed the information gap. Hardware, sensors, fire-safety pillars and gravity regime are not in the data tables. We curated them by hand for all 15 investigations, each field with a character-exact quote and a page or row locator, and with its review status.
  • A clean knowledge base. Of 732 PDFs we index only 20 scientific documents (1,057 pages, 2,390 searchable passages). Engineering drawings, telemetry and image folders are excluded by default, because noise in the index degrades the answers.
  • 9 further public sources (NASA, ESA, ISS National Lab) archived with capture time and checksum.

How it works

  • Orchestrated pipeline (LangGraph): a deterministic ranker scores every investigation for the user's oxygen and pressure; retrieval pulls passages from the curated corpus; one language model writes the explanation; a deterministic validator checks every citation, quote and number before anything is shown. The model never computes a score.
  • Trust by design: unverified claims are withheld, never shown. If too little survives, the user gets the ranking only. Each citation has a View source action that opens the archived NASA document. 480 automated tests, and 279 stress runs with a real model: 73% fully validated, 22% partial (unverified claims withheld), 4% ranking only.
  • Click the chart, get the science: select a point on the oxygen/pressure coverage map and the copilot ranks the closest NASA experiments for that condition. A tidy CSV/JSON export lets users train their own models.

FLAMSA Architectural Design:

FLAMSA RAG DESIGN

AI Orquestration Design:

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python 3.12 (application, data curation, statistics, AI pipeline), HTML/CSS (interface styling), JavaScript/Node.js (automated browser checks), Mermaid (architecture diagrams).
  • Application and data: Streamlit and Altair (dashboard and charts), Pydantic v2 (domain model and validation), pandas, NumPy and SciPy (curation and statistics), scikit-learn (TF-IDF retrieval), pypdf and Poppler (PDF text extraction).
  • AI pipeline: LangGraph and LangChain (orchestration), OpenAI API with gpt-4.1-mini (narration of validated answers).
  • Quality: pytest (481 automated tests), Ruff, mypy.
  • Cloud and delivery: Google Cloud Platform (Cloud Run, Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager), Docker, Git and GitHub.
  • AI assistants used during development: Claude (Claude Code), OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT for coding, review and writing support; Lovable for interface prototyping.
  • Design and media: Figma (interface design), draw.io (orchestration diagram), DaVinci Resolve (video editing).
  • Hardware: a personal Windows 11 computer for development; the public demo runs on Google Cloud Run (1 vCPU, 2 GiB). No special hardware.

Try it: https://www.flamsa.earth (copilot: 4 questions per visitor per day).
